slides.say: A B is tangent to a circle with center O and radius six centimeters. Given, O A equals O B, and angle A O B is ninety degrees. What is the area inside triangle A O B but outside the circle, in square centimeters?
at: A B is tangent to a circle

slides.say: So they ask for the shaded area, the part of the triangle that is outside the circle. [short pause] We'll solve it the math way, and then we'll see two quick exam ways.
at: So they ask for the shaded area

slides.say: [short pause] Let's start with the math way. We met shaded areas in quadrilaterals. We usually find them by subtracting areas, and they come back often in circle questions.
at: Let's start with the math way

slides.say: So first we decide which area to subtract from which. Look at the whole triangle A O B.
Inside it there's a sector of the circle. If we take the triangle and remove the sector, what's left is exactly the shaded part. So the shaded area is the triangle minus the sector.
at: there's a sector of the circle

slides.say: Now let's put in the givens. O A equals O B, so we mark them equal. And the angle at O is ninety degrees.
So triangle A O B isn't just a right triangle. It's right and isosceles, a silver triangle. In a silver triangle, the two base angles are forty-five degrees each.
Next, A B is tangent to the circle. We learned a useful construction for this. When there's a point of tangency, we draw the radius to it. Let's call that point C.
We draw the radius from O to C. The radius is perpendicular to the tangent, so the angle at C is ninety degrees.
at: We draw the radius from O to C

slides.say: Triangle A O B is isosceles, and O C is the height to its base. In an isosceles triangle, this height is also an angle bisector and a median. So it cuts the angle at O into two angles of forty-five degrees.

The radius is six, so O C is six. Triangle O C B has a right angle at C and forty-five degrees at B. So it's a silver triangle too, and C B equals O C, six. On the other side, A C is six too. So A B is six plus six, twelve.
at: and C B equals O C, six
So A B is six plus six

slides.say: Now the triangle's area. The base A B, twelve, and its height O C, six, are already known. So let's use them directly. The area is base times height, over two.
Some students find the two legs of the silver triangle first. We don't need them here, because we already have a base and its height.
Twelve times six is seventy-two. Over two, it's thirty-six. So the triangle is thirty-six.
[pause] Now we could go on and find the sector. But on the exam we also have the choices, and here they help us.

We stop halfway, and we use what we already know to rule out choices. This is called a partial calculation. In this question the triangle is exactly thirty-six. We take away a sector, a quarter of a circle with radius six. Its area is some number times pi. The choices are already written without brackets, with the two area parts separate. So here the answer must be thirty-six, minus some number of pi. If a choice has brackets, expand them before comparing its parts.
at: So here the answer must be

slides.say: Choice number three is eighteen pi minus eighteen. Here the pi part is added, and only eighteen is taken away. That's not thirty-six minus a sector, so it's out.
at: Choice number three is eighteen pi

slides.say: Choice number one is eighteen minus nine pi. The pi part could fit, but our triangle is thirty-six, not eighteen. It's out too.
Choice number four is seventy-two minus nine pi. Seventy-two is twelve times six, with no dividing by two. That's not the triangle either, so it's out.
Only choice number two is left, thirty-six minus nine pi. We started the math way, and stopped halfway to look at the choices. On the exam, we mark it and move on.
at: Only choice number two is left

slides.say: [pause] But we're in a lesson, so let's also find the sector. A sector is a part of the circle. The whole circle is pi r squared. Pi times six squared is thirty-six pi.
Which part? The central angle decides it, and here it's ninety degrees. Ninety out of three hundred sixty is a quarter. A quarter of thirty-six pi is nine pi.
at: Ninety out of three hundred sixty

slides.say: The shaded area is the triangle minus the sector. So it's thirty-six minus nine pi. That's choice number two, the same as before.
at: So it's thirty-six minus nine pi

slides.say: Now let's solve it by estimation. Start from the givens again. The triangle is right and isosceles. The radius O C is six, perpendicular to A B. It cuts the base into two equal parts of six, so A B is twelve. The triangle's area is twelve times six, over two, which is thirty-six.
at: Now let's solve it by estimation

slides.say: The shaded part is only a piece of the triangle. So the shaded area is more than zero, and less than thirty-six.
at: So the shaded area is more than zero

slides.say: Now the choices. We need the size of pi. Pi is a bit more than three, and less than four. So nine pi is more than twenty-seven, and less than thirty-six.
at: Pi is a bit more than three

slides.say: Choice number one, eighteen minus nine pi. Nine pi is more than twenty-seven, so eighteen minus it is less than zero. A negative answer can hide behind letters like this. An area can't be negative, so it's out.

Choice number three, eighteen pi minus eighteen. Eighteen pi is more than eighteen times three, fifty-four. Minus eighteen, it's still more than thirty-six. That's bigger than the whole triangle, so it's out.
at: That's bigger than the whole triangle

slides.say: Choice number four, seventy-two minus nine pi. Nine pi is less than thirty-six, so seventy-two minus it is more than thirty-six. Too big again, it's out.

Choice number two, thirty-six minus nine pi. Nine pi is between twenty-seven and thirty-six, so this is between zero and nine. That's inside our range, more than zero and less than thirty-six. Choice number two again.
Estimating doesn't always rule out three choices. Sometimes it rules out only one or two. Here the two bounds, zero and thirty-six, were enough. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next question.
